results.NEGATIVE_CLAIM: That the word 'discovery' (as the review uses it) does not, and cannot, describe the span of years in which the work went unshown while its maker was alive.
results.SCOPE: Every occurrence of the discover- lexeme in the source: 'undiscovered archives'; 'only discovered after her death in 2013'; 'Another largely undiscovered artist'; 'this previously undiscovered marginalised artist'; 'undiscovered narratives'. Finite and enumerable, and the relevant question is which time each locates.
results.EVIDENCE_OR_METHOD: The source itself splits the two times inside one sentence: 'she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime, and was only discovered after her death in 2013.' The lifetime of non-showing is named by 'never showed... in her lifetime'; the discovery word is placed after death. The same split recurs: Walter 'died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime', Hasegawa's work 'stayed unpublished and unseen in his lifetime' while he is introduced as 'another largely undiscovered artist'. So in this source the discovery word marks the finding, and other words carry the unshown years.
results.WHY_SCOPE_IS_COMPLETE: The proof is not absence-based: the source explicitly assigns the two times to different expressions in the same sentences. The enumeration of all five discovery-family occurrences is a supporting check, not the load-bearing step - none of them names the lifetime span, and the source names that span with separate wording each time.
results.REASON: The 'does not describe' half is explicitly licensed: the source's own sentences put discovery after death and use different wording for the unshown lifetime. The added 'and cannot' is a claim about what the word is capable of meaning - an argument about vocabulary, not a factual property of the review - and the review does report those unshown years in plain terms, so this is not an omission claim. Analysis of source-grounded material with a surviving explicit contrast behind it: INTERPRETATION rather than SUPPORTED, because the modal 'cannot' is not demonstrable from the source, and rather than UNSUPPORTED, because the underlying contrast is stated by the source itself.
